lead: A square-law device — a diode or transistor driven with a small signal — has a current containing the square of its input voltage. Carrier plus message at its input produces sidebands. A band-pass filter then gives AM with carrier. A balanced modulator uses two such devices with the message in antiphase; subtracting outputs cancels the carrier and leaves DSB-SC. Both methods are cheap, need no crystal, and appear in low-power transmitters and radio mixers.
prereq: You need the AM expression, modulation index and spectrum from 2.1, and the idea that a diode or transistor has a nonlinear current–voltage relation.

sections.h3: The square law multiplies two signals

blocks.text: A resistor is linear. A diode or bipolar transistor is not. Around its bias point, its current follows a power series in input voltage.

blocks.where: i is device current in amperes; v is input voltage in volts; a₀ is DC bias current in amperes; a₁ is linear slope in A/V; a₂ is square-law coefficient in A/V²; a₃ and higher terms describe the rest of the curvature.

blocks.text: For a small signal, cube and higher terms are negligible. The device is then square-law. Feed it carrier plus message.
v = A_c cos ω_c t + A_m cos ω_m t
blocks.where: A_c is carrier amplitude in volts; ω_c = 2πf_c is carrier angular frequency in rad/s; A_m is message amplitude in volts; ω_m = 2πf_m is message angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: Substituting v into i = a₀ + a₁v + a₂v² and using cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 and 2cosAcosB = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B) splits the square term into four groups.
a₂v² = a₂A_c²/2 + (a₂A_c²/2)cos 2ω_c t + a₂A_cA_m[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + cos(ω_c + ω_m)t] + a₂A_m²/2 + (a₂A_m²/2)cos 2ω_m t
blocks.where: these are parts of the square term in amperes: first pair is DC and carrier second harmonic; middle pair is the two sidebands; last pair is DC and message second harmonic.

items: Linear term a₁v: copies of carrier at f_c and message at f_m. No new frequencies.
Square term: DC, sidebands at f_c − f_m and f_c + f_m, second harmonics at 2f_c and 2f_m.
Only the cross product A_c cos ω_c t × A_m cos ω_m t makes sidebands. Squaring is the cheapest multiplier.

blocks.text: Sidebands are useful. Everything else is filtered out.
A band-pass filter centred on f_c keeps carrier and sidebands, rejects the rest.

items: Add carrier and message: v = A_c cos ω_c t + A_m cos ω_m t. Figure uses 2 V carrier and 0.5 V tone.
Apply v to the square-law device. Figure uses i = v + 0.2v², so a₁ = 1 A/V and a₂ = 0.2 A/V².
Band-pass filter: centre f_c = 100 kHz, bandwidth 2f_m = 2 kHz. Passes 99–101 kHz; rejects DC, 1 kHz message, 2 kHz harmonic, 200 kHz second harmonic.
Output is AM with carrier amplitude a₁A_c and each sideband amplitude a₂A_cA_m.

blocks.where: m is modulation index, a pure number; a₂ is in A/V²; A_m is in volts; a₁ is in A/V. Standard AM, i = A_c(1 + m cos ω_m t)cos ω_c t, has sidebands A_c m/2 each.

items: m does not depend on A_c. Raising carrier amplitude raises output power, not modulation index.
m rises with message amplitude only while a₃v³ stays small. Practical square-law modulators run at m ≈ 0.2 to 0.5; larger m distorts.
Efficiency is poor: most output power sits in the carrier, which carries no information (see 2.1).
Nearest unwanted product is carrier second harmonic at 2f_c, one octave away, so a simple tuned circuit separates it.

blocks.text: Two identical square-law devices, outputs subtracted. Carrier is fed in phase to both, message in antiphase.
v₁ = A_c cos ω_c t + A_m cos ω_m t,   v₂ = A_c cos ω_c t − A_m cos ω_m t
blocks.where: v₁ and v₂ are the two input voltages in volts; symbols carry the same meaning as before.

blocks.text: i₁ − i₂ = 2a₁A_m cos ω_m t + 2a₂A_cA_m[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]
blocks.where: i₁ − i₂ is difference current in amperes. First term is message at f_m; second term is the pair of sidebands.

blocks.text: Common terms cancel: DC, second harmonic at 2ω_c, second harmonic at 2ω_m, and carrier at ω_c. Message at ω_m survives but is far below f_c and removed by output band-pass filter. Output is DSB-SC.
DSB-SC carries no carrier: saves power but needs coherent detection (see 2.2 and 2.5).
Ring modulator: four diodes in a ring, switched by carrier, message through centre-tapped transformer. Passive, no bias supply, works to hundreds of megahertz.
Matching decides everything. A few percent mismatch leaves residual carrier, wasting power and upsetting the detector.

figure.caption: The 2 V carrier and 0.5 V tone are added, squared by the device, and band-pass filtered to AM around 100 kHz. The output carrier comes from the linear term, not squaring.

spec.title: Square-law AM generator
spec.aria: A 2 V carrier and a 0.5 V tone are added and passed through a square-law device with i = v + 0.2v²; a band-pass filter then selects the AM output around 100 kHz.

examples.question: A square-law device has i = 1.0v + 0.2v², with i in amperes and v in volts. Its input is v = 2cos(2π × 100 × 10³ t) + 0.5cos(2π × 1 × 10³ t) V. The output passes through a band-pass filter centred at 100 kHz with 2 kHz bandwidth. Find carrier current amplitude, amplitude of each sideband, modulation index, and list unwanted products the filter must reject.
steps: Read coefficients and inputs: a₀ = 0, a₁ = 1.0 A/V, a₂ = 0.2 A/V², A_c = 2 V at f_c = 100 kHz, A_m = 0.5 V at f_m = 1 kHz, so ω_c = 2π × 10⁵ rad/s and ω_m = 2π × 10³ rad/s.
Linear term: a₁v = 1.0 × [2cos ω_c t + 0.5cos ω_m t] = 2cos ω_c t + 0.5cos ω_m t A. Carrier amplitude 2 A; message copy at 1 kHz has 0.5 A.
Square term, cross product: a₂ × 2A_cA_m = 0.2 × 2 × 2 × 0.5 = 0.4 A. Using 2cosAcosB = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B): 0.4cos ω_c t cos ω_m t = 0.2cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + 0.2cos(ω_c + ω_m)t A.
Each sideband has amplitude 0.2 A, at 99 kHz and 101 kHz.
Modulation index from amplitudes: m = 2 × (sideband amplitude)/(carrier amplitude) = 2 × 0.2/2 = 0.2, that is 20%.
Check with design formula: m = 2a₂A_m/a₁ = 2 × 0.2 × 0.5/1.0 = 0.2. Same value.
Unwanted products: DC = 0.2 × 2²/2 + 0.2 × 0.5²/2 = 0.4 + 0.025 = 0.425 A; 1 kHz at 0.5 A; 2 kHz at 0.025 A; 200 kHz at 0.4 A. A filter passing 99–101 kHz removes all four.
examples.answer: Carrier 2 A, each sideband 0.2 A, modulation index 0.2 (20%); filter rejects 0.425 A of DC, 0.5 A at 1 kHz, 0.025 A at 2 kHz and 0.4 A at 200 kHz.
examples.check:
a1 = 1.0     # A/V
a2 = 0.2     # A/V^2
Ac = 2.0     # V
Am = 0.5     # V
carrier = a1 * Ac
sideband = a2 * Ac * Am
m = 2 * sideband / carrier
print(carrier)
print(sideband)
print(sideband)
print(m)

traps: The carrier at ω_c comes from the linear term a₁v, not from squaring. The square term alone gives only sidebands, DC and second harmonics.
m = 2a₂A_m/a₁ contains no A_c. Raising carrier amplitude only raises power, not modulation index.
A balanced modulator cancels carrier only when the two halves are matched. Mismatch leaves carrier leakage, a favourite one-mark question.
The message term at ω_m is still present at a balanced modulator output. It is removed by the output band-pass filter, not by balancing.
Square law holds only for a small signal. Large A_m brings in a₃v³, adding sidebands at f_c ± 2f_m and distorting the envelope; keep m small.

quiz.q: Write the power-series model of a square-law device and give the unit of each coefficient.
quiz.a: i = a₀ + a₁v + a₂v², with a₀ in A, a₁ in A/V and a₂ in A/V²; i is in amperes and v in volts.

quiz.q: Why can a perfectly linear amplifier not generate AM sidebands from a carrier and a tone?
quiz.a: Its output is only a scaled copy of the input, so it contains f_c and f_m and nothing else. Sidebands at f_c ± f_m need multiplication of the two signals, and multiplication needs a nonlinear term.

quiz.q: A device has i = 2v + 0.1v² (A, A/V, A/V²) and v = 3cos ω_c t + 0.4cos ω_m t V. Find carrier amplitude, each sideband amplitude and modulation index.
For the same device, message amplitude is raised to 0.8 V. Find new sideband amplitude and modulation index, and state the practical limit.
quiz.a: Sideband = 0.1 × 3 × 0.8 = 0.24 A. m = 2 × 0.24/6 = 0.08. Limit is the a₃v³ term: once the signal is large the device is no longer square law, so extra sidebands and envelope distortion appear.

quiz.q: In a balanced modulator the inputs are v₁ = A_c cos ω_c t + A_m cos ω_m t and v₂ = A_c cos ω_c t − A_m cos ω_m t, and the currents are subtracted. Show which components cancel and which survive.
quiz.a: Linear carrier terms are equal in both currents and cancel. Linear message terms are opposite and add to 2a₁A_m cos ω_m t. DC, 2ω_c and 2ω_m terms are identical and cancel. The cross product flips sign, so it adds to 2a₂A_cA_m[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]: sidebands only, plus the low-frequency message which the filter removes.

quiz.q: A balanced modulator is built with two transistors whose a₁ values differ by 5%. What appears at the output that should not be there, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: The carrier no longer cancels completely; residual carrier leaks out. It wastes transmitter power, and an envelope detector at the receiver would then produce output even without a proper carrier, giving distorted or false recovery.

quiz.q: What is a ring modulator and what is its main advantage?
quiz.a: A balanced modulator made of four diodes in a ring, switched by the carrier, with the message fed through a centre-tapped transformer. It is passive, needs no bias supply, and works at high frequencies.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Gilbert cell inside analog multiplier ICs is a balanced pair of differential pairs — two square-law transistors with outputs subtracted — and is the standard way to multiply in silicon. Diode ring modulators are sold as double-balanced mixers and serve as modulators and mixers from about 1 MHz to several hundred MHz. In software-defined radio the multiplication moves into the digital domain after the ADC, so the analog modulator shrinks to a single mixer stage.
